html:
Surah Al-Baqarah (The Cow) is the second and longest chapter of the Qur’an — 286 verses revealed in Madinah over roughly nine years. It is the first full surah the Prophet (✌) received in the new city, and its last two verses were the final passage of the entire Qur’an revealed through a different route: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that an angel descended with them from a gate of heaven never opened before, announcing “Rejoice in two lights given to you that were never given to any prophet before you: the Opening of the Book and the concluding verses of Surah al-Baqarah” (Sahih Muslim 806).

Those closing two verses — 285 and 286, known across the Muslim world as Āmanar-Rasūl after their opening words — carry a direct promise from the Prophet (✌): “Whoever recites the last two verses of Surah al-Baqarah in a night, they will suffice him” (Sahih al-Bukhari 5009, also Bukhari 5040 and Muslim 807, Agreed Upon). The Arabic word is kafatāhu — from kifāyah, “sufficiency” — and classical commentators including al-Nawawī and Ibn Hajar hold the sufficiency to cover both the night’s protection and standing in place of qiyām al-layl for one who could not pray it.

Verse 285 is the believer’s creed in one sentence: belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the refusal to distinguish between any of them. Verse 286 opens with the covenantal clause la yukallifu-Llāhu nafsan illā wusʿahā — “Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity” — and closes with a five-part duʿā that is one of the most-recited supplications in Islam: forgiveness for forgetfulness and error, protection from burdens like those of previous nations, pardon, mercy, and victory over disbelief.

Ibn Kathīr, in his tafsir of these two ayat, notes that each petition in verse 286 was answered on the spot — Allah accepted the duʿā phrase by phrase (the naʿam, naʿam narration, cited by Muslim 126). This is why the two verses are standard in the Prophetic bedtime routine on this site’s duʿā collection: they are both dhikr and shield. If you memorise anything from al-Baqarah in your lifetime, memorise these two — four short minutes of recitation a night.
